The Science of Laughter

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In South Africa’s most overstretched hospitals, a small band of entertainers is proving that laughter isn’t just comic relief — it may be a quiet, evidence-backed form of medicine.

Unique Selling Point:
They arrive with red noses, music, jokes and oversized energy ,but what the Laughter Heroes do is far more than entertainment.
At Lombano Hospice, Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital, and Helen Joseph Hospital, a small group of trained performers regularly enter some of the most emotionally and physically demanding spaces in South African healthcare. Their job is simple: make sick children laugh. The impact, however, may be far more complex — and scientifically significant.
For decades, laughter has been associated with improved wellbeing. From reduced stress hormones and lowered blood pressure, to improved immune response and pain tolerance, international research increasingly suggests that humour and play can be powerful therapeutic tools — particularly for children undergoing long, invasive, and frightening medical treatments. This is not the romanticised version popularised by Patch Adams; this is structured, intentional intervention in clinical environments.
We speak to paediatric oncologists Dr Thandeka Ngcana from Bara and Wits Lecturer and , palliative care specialists and psychologists who work alongside Laughter Heroes and have observed tangible changes in their patients: reduced anxiety before procedures, improved cooperation with treatment, better mood regulation, and in some cases, faster recovery times. Dr Ngcana will speak anecdotally but critically ,drawing on real case studies and years of frontline experience, while referencing peer-reviewed research that supports these observations.
At Lombano Hospice, laughter becomes a tool for dignity and relief at end-of-life care. At Bara and Helen Joseph, it helps children reclaim moments of childhood in sterile, intimidating hospital wards. For parents and staff, the presence of Laughter Heroes often shifts the emotional temperature of entire wards ,easing burnout and restoring humanity in spaces dominated by illness.
We follow the Laughter Heroes themselves The Marvelous Stewart Mcnab(A…lets just say a quite boisterous clown and the rather awkward clown Themba Mathabela) ,trained practitioners who understand boundaries, trauma, and timing. Their work requires emotional intelligence, resilience, and an ability to read medical environments in real time. This is not performance for applause, but precision interaction designed to support healing.
Through observational filming, expert interviews, and case studies, this story looks at whether laughter can be measured, studied, and respected as part of modern medicine and why South Africa’s most overstretched hospitals may need it now more than ever.

Script:


(Claire) Hospitals are always busy, nobody really plans to be here.
There are long queues, a lot of serious faces… and of course, needles…
(Claire) It’s especially scary when you’re the tiniest of patients.
(Claire) But something strange is happening in paediatric wards across the country.
(Stewart Kaan) Come, come.
(Themba Mathabela) Hi, hi.
(Claire) In some of the most demanding corners of healthcare,
(Stewart Kaan) Big high five, yay.
(Claire) laughter is finding its way in.
(Dr Thandeka Ngcana) In some cases, we prescribe laughter.
(Themba Mathabela) Pull, pull.
(Claire) And it’s having surprisingly positive effects.
(Themba Mathabela) Yebo.
(Claire) In hospital wards defined by long queues, anxiety, needles and machines, laughter can feel out of place — but what if it’s introduced deliberately, and could it be doing more than we realise?
(Claire) At one of Johannesburg’s busiest hospitals, Charlotte Maxeke, laughter has been part of paediatric oncology care for nearly a decade, thanks to the Laughter Heroes.
(Stewart Kaan) Come on guys, come on.
(Themba Mathabela) Come join us.
(Claire) An initiative by Reach For A Dream, the Laughter Heroes are specially trained performers who work alongside doctors and nurses — using humour and magic tricks to help children cope with treatment and make hospital life a little less scary.
(Stewart Kaan) Go Kayla, abracadabra, louder, louder.
(Kayla) Abracadabra.
(Stewart Kaan) Abracadabra.
(Claire) It's check-up day in Paediatric Oncology. I’m joining two Laughter Heroes — “Uncle Sweet Things” and “Big Max” — on their rounds.
(Stewart Kaan) There’s Orangie, there’s my pal, how are you? How are you?
(Themba Mathabela) Hello, hello, how are you?
(Stewart Kaan) What must I make you? I can guess. I am going to make a sword.
(Themba Mathabela) So, what are we going to make, a flower or a rose?
(Stewart Kaan) You are going to be a fighter — a warrior by the time this is made.
(Claire) It’s a tough crowd…
(Themba Mathabela) Ok, it’s fine, you're going to have that.
(Stewart Kaan) It didn't look like a sword in the beginning, but look at that.
(Claire) But the kids soon warm up.
(Stewart Kaan) There you go, just for you.
(Stewart Kaan) Sword fight.
(Claire) For the medical staff, they are always a welcome sight.
(Claire) Doctor Thandeka Ngcana, the country’s only dedicated paediatric neuro-oncologist, often calls on the Laughter Heroes while working with patients.
(Claire) Paint a picture for someone who doesn't understand how a Laughter Hero enters the space between the doctor and the patient?
(Dr Thandeka Ngcana) I come with the medicine, I come with the drips, with the antibiotics and the chemotherapy…
(Claire) All the scary stuff.
(Dr Thandeka Ngcana) All the scary stuff. But here is this person who walks into the room and comes with things that make oncology children normal children. While patients are waiting to be seen by the doctors, the Laughter Heroes will start to play with them, they will start the interaction with them, they will start with — you know — a magic trick show. I have walked into rooms where I am examining a patient and the child was just so scared, and the Laughter Hero walked in with a balloon and for some weird reason there was a major transition and this child becomes a brand new child and he’s forgotten that I am poking the tummy, that I’m listening to the chest.
(Claire) It isn’t a cure, but in these wards, Dr Ngcana sees it making a real difference.
(Dr Thandeka Ngcana) There is a science in it. I feel that a happy child heals better. The endorphins — your stress hormones — because of less anxiety, you are stressing yourself less, and in the long term you heal better. It also helps as a distraction in some of the kids — they’re in isolation because of the complications of the treatment, because of the diagnosis they have.
(Dr Thandeka Ngcana) So let’s say the patient has got edema…
(Dr Thandeka Ngcana) You can't say I didn't teach you anything in your whole life.
(Claire) She’s also teaching the next generation of doctors that laughter has a place in medicine.
(Dr Thandeka Ngcana) In medical school, a long, long time ago, we were taught that for any approach in patient care you have to have a bio-psycho-social approach. Now I come in with the biology stuff, and then in some cases, we prescribe laughter.
(Claire) “Uncle Sweet Things” is the longest-serving Laughter Hero. Away from the wards, he’s just Themba Mathabela, a trained theatre actor and acting coach… and every morning starts the same way.
(Claire) How did you get into that space of performance?
(Themba Mathabela) The things I was doing as a young boy, you could tell this is a natural performer because I used to imitate a lot of people when the stories were playing. As I grew, I came across sketches, industrial theatres, protest theatres, so I fell in love with that when I saw people doing it.
(Claire) In 2015, Reach For A Dream invited Themba to become a Laughter Hero.
(Claire) What, as a performer, must you take into consideration when you are going to perform for children who are not well?
(Themba Mathabela) We try our level best to make it a point that we leave a positive impact at the end of the day. Whatever you're giving — it's not tangible, but it's more authentic. It's just having to be you — yourself — give the love you can, as much as you can. That's the beautiful part. And that's the most challenging part again.
(Stewart Kaan) The great thing about magic is magic transcends every barrier. It transcends every culture. It transcends every age group. Whether I'm performing to geriatrics or paediatrics, it doesn't matter.
(Claire) A favourite with the medical team, he’s known as “Big Max.” But when the jacket comes off, he’s Stewart Kaan — a performer with a passion for magic and mentalism.
(Claire) Laughter Heroes go where the need is greatest. At Lambano Hospice in Germiston, east of Joburg, today they are needed more than ever.
(Claire) On the schedule today for the Laughter Heroes was a visit to this hospice. On arrival, the mood was quite somber with the caregivers because a child lost their life just last night. This difficult situation is what the Laughter Heroes face every single day.
(Themba Mathabela) Morning, morning.
(Stewart Kaan) One, two, three.
(Claire) They don’t wait — Big Max works his magic with the medical staff… while Uncle Sweet Things runs storytime and balloon duty.
(Stewart Kaan) I was naive. I used to think that death and illness only happen to older people. But in this job, you see. And it is terribly sad when a 4- or 5-year-old is stricken. The ethos is to create hope.
(Themba Mathabela) There are times you feel like quitting. I don't know, because you're like, I can't save those children, I can't — even if I try as much as I can for those kids. We made a commitment that we will be there for you.
(Claire) For 12-year-old Fransiska van Niekerk, chronic kidney disease makes every day a challenge. But magic, laughter, and the simple joy of being a child again — these are the moments that stay with her the longest.
(Claire) So tell me about the guys that would come here and entertain you with magic and balloons.
(Fransiska) First time I was very, very scared. I wanted my mother to sleep with me and stuff. But after that they started to make myself happy and stuff. Every time I see them, I go to them.
(Claire) Did you enjoy that?
(Fransiska) Yes. Last time when he came, when I was here, they told us that we must close our eyes. He will make us disappear. After that, then all of us, we close our eyes. Then he said, open your eyes. After that, then you say, okay, the guys are done disappearing. That's what I like about them.
(Stewart Kaan) High five, high five.
(Claire) This is the Heroes’ purpose. Every day they enter the hardest spaces with courage. And no matter the challenge, they show up for the moments that matter most.
(Themba Mathabela) Say, I believe this is a few children...
(Parent) I believe...
(Themba Mathabela) I love that…
(Stewart Kaan) I love it.
(Themba Mathabela) I’m so grateful that my presence contributes towards their health and well-being at the end of the day as well. Not just them having balloons, seeing magic and all these things, but then it releases them. It makes them free again as kids at the end of the day.
(Stewart Kaan) You know, I've had a great life. I've travelled the world, I performed in many, many places. And I cannot think of something better to give back to these stricken children — and that is hope and laughter.

We speak to paediatric oncologists Dr Thandeka Ngcana from Bara and Wits Lecturer and , palliative care specialists and psychologists who work alongside Laughter Heroes and have observed tangible changes in their patients: reduced anxiety before procedures, improved cooperation with treatment, better mood regulation, and in some cases, faster recovery times. Dr Ngcana will speak anecdotally but critically ,drawing on real case studies and years of frontline experience, while referencing peer-reviewed research that supports these observations. At Lombano Hospice, laughter becomes a tool for dignity and relief at end-of-life care. At Bara and Helen Joseph, it helps children reclaim moments of childhood in sterile, intimidating hospital wards. For parents and staff, the presence of Laughter Heroes often shifts the emotional temperature of entire wards ,easing burnout and restoring humanity in spaces dominated by illness. We follow the Laughter Heroes themselves The Marvelous Stewart Mcnab(A…lets just say a quite boisterous clown and the rather awkward clown Themba Mathabela) ,trained practitioners who understand boundaries, trauma, and timing. Their work requires emotional intelligence, resilience, and an ability to read medical environments in real time. This is not performance for applause, but precision interaction designed to support healing. Through observational filming, expert interviews, and case studies, this story looks at whether laughter can be measured, studied, and respected as part of modern medicine and why South Africa’s most overstretched hospitals may need it now more than ever.
